# Isaiah 37: Research Notes for a Verse-by-Verse Commentary

**A note on gaps first.** I couldn't find any verse in these sources where Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed or Lutheran teachers clearly disagree in their own words. The main place where interpreters differ is how the army died in v. 36. I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter, and nothing from oca.org, so those are left out. I only name a commentator's tradition when the page names it.

---

**v. 1** – Guzik says Hezekiah's first reaction was right because he saw the situation as it really was. His next step was even better: he did not let grief turn him away from the LORD. Hezekiah's initial reaction is good. He sees the situation for what it really is... Hezekiah's second reaction was even better. He did not allow his mourning and grief to spin him into a rejection of the LORD's power and help. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-37/
- The Pulpit Commentary says that by putting on sackcloth Hezekiah showed deeper grief than his officials had. The temple was also a "house of prayer," and he went there only to pray. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm
- Gill says trouble should not keep persons from, but bring them to, the house of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-1.htm
- Matthew Henry: Rabshakeh intended to frighten Hezekiah from the Lord, but it proves that he frightens him to the Lord. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_037.cfm

**v. 2** – Pulpit calls this a dignified embassy, showing how much Isaiah was held in honour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-2.htm
- Ellicott says the prophet people had once mocked was now their only hope. In that supreme hour of calamity the prophet, who had been despised and derided, was their one resource. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-2.htm
- Barnes: the priests wore mourning because the God they served had been insulted and the temple itself was threatened. (Same URL.)
- Oswalt, quoted on Precept Austin, wonders whether Isaiah and Shebna looked at each other, both remembering when Isaiah had foretold Shebna's fall (Isa 22:15-19). https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-37-commentary

**v. 3** – Pulpit reads "rebuke" as a rebuke from God on Judah. Hezekiah himself deserved it for relying on Egypt for so long. Pulpit argues the word means "blasphemy." It calls the birth image a common saying for a time of extreme difficulty, and says the picture shouldn't be pressed too far. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm
- Guzik: the image expressed the total calamity of the situation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-37/

**v. 4** – Pulpit: "the living God" is set against dead idols. The "remnant" may mean the people still in the land, as opposed to the many already carried off. It notes that Sennacherib's annals claim 46 cities taken and over 200,000 captives. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the phrase sounds like a comparison of Rabshakeh to Goliath. They add that the deliverance of the remnant is a key-note of Isaiah's prophecies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-1.htm
- Precept Austin: Because the crisis concerns God's glory, the proper response is intercession, not strategy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-37-commentary

**v. 5** – Barnes on "will hear": God will act to defend his name against the reproach, as "hear" is used in Exodus 2:24. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-5.htm

**v. 6** – Guzik senses a gentle rebuke here: Rabshakeh's words are only words. Perhaps we can sense the gentlest rebuke in these words from the LORD. He also notes that this first word does not yet promise the city's rescue. It is aimed at Rabshakeh personally. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-37/
- Pulpit: the word for "servants" is a scornful one. Cheyne renders it "minions"; Pulpit suggests "lackeys." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm

**v. 7** – Pulpit: "a spirit" means God would replace the king's pride with hesitation and fear. Interpreters disagree about the "rumour": it may be news about Tirhakah, news of the army's destruction, or both. Pulpit rejects the idea of a revolt elsewhere in the empire, saying there is no evidence for it. It also says the promise was deliberately vague at first, with details given later in vv. 22-35. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm
- Precept Austin sees the prophecy as specific: withdrawal, then death by the sword at home. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-37-commentary

**v. 8** – Pulpit: Libnah was near Lachish, its exact site is unknown, and it was probably the next stronghold on the way to Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm
- Guzik: Hezekiah may have thought Rabshakeh's withdrawal was the promise already coming true. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-37/

**v. 9** – Pulpit: Tirhakah ruled Ethiopia and was overlord of the Nile valley from about 700 BC. Hezekiah had probably been negotiating with him. Pulpit thinks his advance annoyed Sennacherib more than it worried him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm

**v. 10** – Pulpit: Sennacherib accepted the LORD as a god, but only as one of the gods of the nations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm
- Guzik: lumping the LORD in with the nations' gods was blasphemy that invited judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-37/

**v. 11** – Pulpit quotes Assyrian kings' inscriptions in which they claim to rule the whole world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm
- Henry: Great successes often harden sinners' hearts in their sinful ways and make them the more daring. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_037.cfm

**vv. 12–13** – Pulpit explains the places. Assyrian kings called all earlier kings their "fathers." Gozan was in upper Mesopotamia, Haran was Abraham's Haran, and the "children of Eden" were probably the people of Bit-Adini on the Euphrates. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm

**v. 14** – Pulpit: Hezekiah spread out the letter so that God would take note of it, not because God needed to read it. Delitzsch called the act a kind of "prayer without words." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm
- Henry: it is worse to write so, for this argues more deliberation and design. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_037.cfm
- Ligonier: Hezekiah did not use this promise as an excuse for inaction. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/Sennacherib-Defeated

**vv. 15–16** – Pulpit: "enthroned above the cherubim" refers to God dwelling between the cherubim in the Holy of Holies. Pulpit argues against critics (Kuenen, Cheyne) who doubt that Hezekiah held such a clear belief in one God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm
- Guzik: calling God Creator acknowledges his power and his rights over everything he made. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-37/

**v. 17** – Pulpit: This is a conscious pleading of the promise made to Solomon (2 Chronicles 7:15). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm

**vv. 18–19** – Pulpit: Assyria's conquests were a stubborn fact, which it was impossible to deny. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the line of thought is that Assyria destroyed those gods because they were only made by human hands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-14.htm

**v. 20** – Pulpit: God's true servants want rescue for the glory of God, that his honour may be vindicated in the sight of the world at large. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-20.htm
- Ryrie, quoted on Precept Austin: the prayer asks only that His glory be vindicated. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-37-commentary

**v. 21** – This is a difference of emphasis about prayer, not a split between denominations:
- Guzik (enduringword.com) says that without the prayer no answer would have come, and Jerusalem would have been conquered. Hezekiah's prayer really mattered. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-37/
- Matthew Henry says Hezekiah probably doubted not but that the issue would be comfortable, yet he would have it to be so in answer to prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_037.cfm

**v. 22** – Motyer, quoted by Guzik: "virgin" means untouched by the attacker, who came intending to violate her. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-37/
- Pulpit: Jerusalem is pictured as a tender maiden who still defies Sennacherib and shakes her head "after him" as he leaves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm

**v. 23** – Biblehub's study notes: no human power can stand against the Almighty. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/isaiah/37.htm

**vv. 24–25** – Pulpit: the emphatic, repeated "I" in the Hebrew marks the proud egotism of the monarch. The armies climbed mountains for plunder, not just for the route. Pulpit points out that "I will dry up" Egypt's streams is still future, while the other boasts are past. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm

**v. 26** – Pulpit: conquerors are mere instruments in God's hands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm
- Henry says it is intolerable arrogance to make it thy own doing. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_037.cfm
- Guzik: the Assyrians owed their success to the LORD without knowing it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-37/

**v. 27** – Ellicott: grass on the housetops was a proverbial emblem of weakness. Gill: the nations fell because the LORD had taken away their strength, not because Sennacherib was strong. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-27.htm

**v. 29** – Guzik: the hook and bit were the very way the Assyrians humiliated their captives, so their own cruelty is turned back on them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-37/

**v. 30** – Interpreters disagree about the timing of the sign:
- Barnes: the sign points to the security that would follow. The sign, therefore, does not refer so much to the past, as to the security and future prosperity which would be consequent thereon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-30.htm
- JFB, following Rosenmüller, takes the first two years as already past. The fact that Sennacherib moved his camp away immediately after shows that the first two years refer to the past, not to the future. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Isa/Isa_037.cfm
- Keil & Delitzsch disagree with JFB: it is only a "sign" if the second year was still to come. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-30.htm
- Gill thinks the second year may have been a sabbatical year. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nas/isaiah/37-30.html
- The Cambridge Bible doubts the sign fixes how long Assyria stayed. It thinks the sign refers to wider damage, such as a depopulated land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-30.htm
- NET note: the sign is a future reminder of God's intervention designated before the actual intervention takes place. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Isa&chapter=37&verse=30

**v. 31** – Pulpit: "take root downward" means the people would spread over the land and flourish again, after Assyria had emptied the countryside. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/37.htm
- Biblehub's study notes connect the remnant theme to Paul in Romans 9:27. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/isaiah/37.htm

**v. 32** – Guzik: God will preserve His remnant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-37/

**vv. 33–34** – Pulpit: there would be no siege at all; he would go back by the coast road. When last heard of he was at Libnah, 30–40 miles away. Pulpit says the verse captures the stages of an Assyrian siege: archers, then shields, then ramps. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-33.htm

**v. 35** – Guzik: David had been dead almost 300 years, yet God kept his promise. Jerusalem deserved judgment, and God acted for his own sake, much as he blesses believers for Christ's sake. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-37/
- Delitzsch links "for mine own sake" to Isaiah 43:25 and 48:11. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-33.htm

**v. 36** – Commentators differ on how the army died:
- **Plague:** Ellicott says the wording allows for disease, and that Isaiah saw it as nothing else than the "angel of the Lord." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-36.htm
- **Against plague:** Barnes argues plague doesn't kill this quickly, and Jerusalem's people would not have stripped plague-ridden bodies. (Same URL.)
- **Storm:** JFB points to a storm of hail and lightning (Isa 29:6; 30:30). (Same URL.)
- **Angel's direct act:** Gill says it shows the power and strength of an angel. (Same URL.)
- **A Wesleyan voice:** Benson, labelled on the page as "Arminian 1811 Wesleyan/Methodist," cites Josephus on pestilence and Vitringa's view that lightning killed them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/19-35.html
- **Wind:** Clarke, on the same page, thinks the "angel" was simply a suffocating or pestilential WIND. (Same URL.)
- **Where it happened:** Pulpit thinks it struck Sennacherib's own main army, probably not near Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-36.htm
- **Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia says the army was stricken by the angel of the Lord, and reports Herodotus's Egyptian story of mice. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/02007c.htm
- Catholic.com raises the possibility that it was plague, since plague is elsewhere described as a blow from God's angel. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/did-angels-really-battle-israels-enemies

**v. 37** – JFB: Sennacherib lived about twenty more years, according to the inscriptions. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Isa/Isa_037.cfm
- Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey): in 701 Hezekiah gave in to Assyria's demands (2 Kgs 18:14-16), and the city being spared was celebrated as divine intervention. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/hezekiah/
- Sennacherib's prism claims he shut Hezekiah up "like a caged bird." https://bible-history.bibleodyssey.org/articles/babylonian-accounts-of-the-invasion-of-judah/
- Biblehub's study notes: the Assyrian account does not claim the capture of Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/study/2_kings/18-13.htm

**v. 38** – Ligonier: Assyria believed its gods to be mighty, but they could not save the Assyrian king even in their own house. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/Sennacherib-Defeated
- MacLaren: Retribution comes slowly, for twenty years intervened between the catastrophe to the army and the murder of the king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/37-33.htm
- Henry: the sons who should have guarded him killed him before the idol whose protection he was seeking. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_037.cfm
